- Model consistently overestimates early in the forecast horizon, especially for the first 5–10 days, then gradually converges toward true values — suggesting a lag or delayed response to market signals.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., 80+), model forecasts overshoot and remain elevated longer than true values, indicating failure to capture mean reversion or policy-induced price corrections.
- Model underestimates true values in the latter half of the forecast (e.g., 25–30 days), particularly when true values show upward momentum or recovery — suggesting a bias toward conservative or downward-looking assumptions.
- Model exhibits persistent bias toward higher prices in the first 10–15 days of the forecast, even when historical data shows clear downward trends — indicating a failure to adjust for recent volatility or policy shocks.
- Model fails to capture sudden downward corrections (e.g., 60–65 range) after initial spikes — suggesting poor sensitivity to short-term policy or supply-demand shocks.
- Model tends to smooth out volatility, underestimating sharp drops or spikes in true values — indicating a lack of granularity in capturing market sentiment or regulatory changes.
- Model’s forecast curve often lags behind true values by 3–5 days, suggesting a delay in adjusting to new information or a structural lag in model calibration.
- Model overcorrects after initial price drops, leading to prolonged overestimation — suggesting a failure to recognize the natural reversion to mean or the persistence of market anomalies.
